"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4352 (layer 15 MLP down projection).

What it is: one rank-one piece of the down projection. Its activation is a linear readout
of the layer's MLP hidden units, spread over many of them with no clean concept behind it.
Its activation is small (mean about 0.02, spread about 0.28) and essentially unpredictable
from the tokens: a per-token lookup, per-character-class means and position in a document
each leave almost all of the variance unexplained.

What this program predicts: only the coarse shape that is there.
- The first token of a document: the component is silent (about 0).
- The second token of a document: a little above average.
- Every other token: its mean level, about 0.02.

Documents are tracked by their document ids, and a row starts a new count at its first token.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

FIRST_TOKEN = 0.0
SECOND_TOKEN = 0.09
OTHER_TOKENS = 0.02


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        index = 0
    else:
        index = carry[1] + 1
    if index == 0:
        value = FIRST_TOKEN
    elif index == 1:
        value = SECOND_TOKEN
    else:
        value = OTHER_TOKENS
    return (doc, index), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 4354: a weak component whose activation sits a
little below zero almost everywhere, dips further at line and sentence breaks (newlines,
'.', '!', '?', '。', ...), and dips furthest at a break whose token already occurred in
the last 64 tokens of its document (repetitive, list-like or keyword-stuffed text).

Rules, reading only the text so far:
  a break that repeats a token from the recent window -> -0.3
  any other break                                    -> -0.2
  any other token                                    -> -0.09 (its typical level)

This captures only about 1% of the activation's variance (eval: r = 0.08). The large
negative spikes depend on context (spam, mixed-language junk, repeated lists) that these
rules do not model. The level it sits at matters more to the model's next-token loss
than the dips do: predicting the typical level keeps cross entropy near switching the
component off, while full-strength dips make it worse.
"""

READS = ()

BREAKS = {".", "!", "?", "。", "！", "？", "…", "..", "..."}
WINDOW = 64


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    i = prefix.position
    tok = prefix.token_strings[i]
    if not ("\n" in tok or tok.strip() in BREAKS):
        return carry, -0.09
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    start = i
    while start > 0 and i - start < WINDOW and docs[start - 1] == docs[i]:
        start -= 1
    if tok in prefix.token_strings[start:i]:
        return carry, -0.3
    return carry, -0.2

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4355.

It is one rank-one direction that layer 15's MLP writes into the residual stream: it reads
the MLP's hidden activations through a dense vector (hidden unit 4355 alone carries about
16% of its variance, but most of it is spread over thousands of units), and writes a fixed
vector back.

What the component does: almost nothing that a reader can name. Its activation is a diffuse,
roughly Gaussian value (mean about -0.01, std 0.29). It is essentially inert: its causal
importance is ~0 at every position and switching it off moves the model's next-token
distribution by about 1e-6 nats. Token identity, token category (word, punctuation, digits,
CJK, code), the previous one or two tokens, repeated tokens and repeated bigrams all explain
under 0.5% of its variance on held-out positions. Its variance is in the bulk of the
distribution, not in rare spikes.

So this program predicts the component's typical value, using the only structure found: the
first token of each document carries essentially zero activation (the MLP has nothing to
read yet), and the second token is slightly negative on average. Everywhere else it predicts
the mean.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN = -0.0125  # typical activation at ordinary positions
SECOND_TOKEN = -0.11  # mean activation of a document's second token


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # carry: the token's index within its document, from the previous step
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    if carry is None or ids[-1] != ids[-2]:
        index = 0  # first token of a document (or of the row)
    else:
        index = carry + 1
    if index == 0:
        value = 0.0
    elif index == 1:
        value = SECOND_TOKEN
    else:
        value = MEAN
    return index, value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 4356: predicts a constant, its typical activation.

The component's activation (its contribution along its read direction) has no concept
behind it that we could name. It averages about -0.095 with spread 0.3, and it is diffuse:
token identity does not predict it on held-out text (R^2 below 0), and coarse token classes
(words, punctuation, digits, CJK, whitespace), and position in the document, explain
about 0.2% of its variance or less. It almost never passes the causal-importance threshold
(0 of 10M tokens), and switching it off barely changes the model. So the program predicts
its typical value at every position. Matching the mean keeps the model's average
contribution from this component, and does better on the model's output than predicting 0.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL_ACTIVATION = -0.095


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, TYPICAL_ACTIVATION

"""Words for things moving or being passed along a system (flow, transfer,
transmission, connection), with a fading memory of them.

The component is positive on words such as flow, transfer, transmission,
connected, coupled, chain, pipeline, circuit, pathway, conduit, relay, signal,
downstream, bypass, and on parts of such networks (pipes, valves, vessels,
cables, transformers, amplifiers). It is most positive on the word itself, and
stays a little above zero for a few tokens after one, so "information flow"
or "supply chain" lift the words that come next. Chinese/Japanese 流 (flow),
链 (chain), 传输 (transmit) and 连接 (connect) count too.

step() returns 1.8 on such a word and 0.6 times a fading memory of recent
ones (decay 0.9 per token, reset at each document boundary). Every other
token gets the memory alone. This explains only about 1% of the variance: most
of the component's activity is not tied to any word.
"""

READS = ()

# Words (matched at their start) naming flow, transfer and connection, and
# the parts of a conduit, circuit or vessel.
FLOW_STEMS = (
    "flow", "transmi", "transfer", "transport", "connect", "couple", "chain",
    "pipe", "circuit", "pathway", "conduit", "channel", "relay", "signal",
    "rout", "stream", "bypass", "cascade", "conveyor", "linkage", "circulat",
    "duct", "drain", "pump", "inlet", "outlet", "exhaust", "amplifier",
    "transformer", "upstream", "downstream", "indirect", "mediat",
    "vein", "vessel", "vascular", "lymph", "arter", "cable", "wire", "valve",
    "hose", "gear", "resistor", "capacitor", "receiver", "router", "neuron",
)
CHINESE_WORDS = ("流", "链", "传输", "连接")
CURRENT = 1.8
MEMORY = 0.6
DECAY = 0.9


def is_flow_token(token):
    word = token.strip().lower()
    if word.isascii() and word.isalpha():
        return word.startswith(FLOW_STEMS)
    return any(part in token for part in CHINESE_WORDS)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    memory = carry or 0.0
    if len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        memory = 0.0
    hit = 1.0 if is_flow_token(prefix.token_strings[-1]) else 0.0
    value = CURRENT * hit + MEMORY * memory
    return DECAY * memory + hit, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 4359: a weak, mostly digit-driven signal.

What it does, in plain terms
- Inside a number, it responds to the position of the current digit within the
  digit run and to the character that opens the run:
  * the first digit after a decimal point, colon, dash or slash is positive,
    and the second digit after a decimal point is more positive;
  * the third digit of a digit run that follows a comma, point, dash, colon or
    slash (e.g. the "4" in 1,234 or the third decimal place) is strongly negative;
  * other digits are about zero.
- A letter-run piece written without a leading space (a piece of a longer word
  split across tokens, e.g. "ent" in "inel") is weakly positive.
- Everything else (spaced words, punctuation, spaces) is about zero.

Why: the component's activation has no clean token identity or context rule
(its per-token means explain nothing held out); these few rules explain only
a small part of its variance, and they are the largest group means found in
the activation data. Predicting the group means is the best a simple rule can do.
"""
import re

READS = ()

DIGIT = re.compile(r"\d")
UNSPACED_LETTERS = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+")
OPENERS = {".", ",", "-", ":", "/"}  # characters that can start a number group


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = toks[-1]
    if DIGIT.fullmatch(t):
        # count the digits already in this run, within the same document
        k, j = 0, len(toks) - 2
        while j >= 0 and docs[j] == docs[-1] and DIGIT.fullmatch(toks[j]):
            k += 1
            j -= 1
        opener = toks[j] if j >= 0 and docs[j] == docs[-1] else ""
        if k == 0 and opener in {".", "-", ":", "/"}:
            return carry, 0.7
        if k == 1 and opener == ".":
            return carry, 1.0
        if k == 2 and opener in OPENERS:
            return carry, -1.2
        return carry, 0.0
    if UNSPACED_LETTERS.fullmatch(t):
        return carry, 0.1
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15's MLP hidden unit 4360, which is this component (its activation is that unit's
value times about 1.1). The unit is diffuse: its large negative spikes depend on context this
program cannot see, and no word-level rule explains more than about 1% of its variance. The
rule below captures the readable part, with each value set to that group's average activation:

- Comparison words ("similar", "same", "compared", "than", "as", ...) dip negative, most of
  all when they directly follow a lead word that sets up a comparison ("similar to", "same as").
- Month names dip negative.
- "the" dips slightly negative, and strongly when it follows such a lead word.
- Words that introduce a spread of alternatives ("between", "among", "various") sit positive.
- A word right after a lead word ("according to", "except for") dips negative.
"""

READS = ()

COMPARE = {" similar", " same", " compared", " comparison", " contrast", " identical",
           " comparable", " different", " unlike", " like", " than", " as"}
LEADS = COMPARE | {" according", " except", " unless", " beyond"}
MONTHS = {" January", " February", " March", " April", " May", " June", " July",
          " August", " September", " October", " November", " December"}
SPREAD = {" between", " among", " various", " several", " depending", " respectively",
          " variety", " across"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    after_lead = prev in LEADS
    if cur in COMPARE:
        value = -3.1 if after_lead else -0.9
    elif cur in MONTHS:
        value = -1.7
    elif cur in SPREAD:
        value = 0.9
    elif cur == " the":
        value = -1.3 if after_lead else -0.36
    else:
        value = -0.58 if after_lead else -0.09
    return carry, value

"""Alternatives-and-lists detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 4361.

What the component does (measured on training text): its output direction promotes
"or"/"either" when its activation is negative, and its negative values occur where a
choice or list is being built: on "or"/"either"/"nor" themselves, on "one"/"some"/"any"
(as in "one of", "one or more"), and on a comma that is the second or later comma of a
sentence (a list of items, where "or"/"and" may come next). Shortly after an "or" or
"whether" its value is weakly positive.

This program is a small rule set over the text so far. It does not see the next token,
so it can only guess where the list or choice is; it captures only a little of the
variance (most of the activation is small and not explained by words).
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

ALTERNATIVE_WORDS = {" or", " Or", " either", " nor"}
ALT_OR_WHETHER = ALTERNATIVE_WORDS | {" whether"}
QUANTIFIERS = {" one", " some", " any"}
SENTENCE_END = {".", ";", "!", "?", "\n", "\n\n"}

NEGATIVE = -0.5  # at a choice word, or a list comma
POSITIVE = 0.15  # a few tokens after "or" / "whether"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Activation at the newest token, from the sentence's comma count and the distance
    since the last "or"-type word (both reset at a new document)."""
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    commas, dist = (0, 99) if carry is None or new_doc else carry
    dist = 0 if tok in ALT_OR_WHETHER else min(dist + 1, 99)
    if tok in ALTERNATIVE_WORDS or tok in QUANTIFIERS:
        value = NEGATIVE
    elif tok == "," and commas >= 1:
        value = NEGATIVE
    elif 1 <= dist <= 6:
        value = POSITIVE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    if tok in SENTENCE_END:
        commas = 0
    elif tok == ",":
        commas += 1
    return (commas, dist), value

"""Ratio and comparison set-ups, negative side.

Component 4362 of layers.15.mlp.down_proj. Most of the time its activation is small and
diffuse. Its large negative values sit on the connecting words of a ratio or a comparison
of two quantities: "to" in "surface area to volume" or "relative to", "per" in "miles per
hour", the "-to" of "warmth-to-weight", "with" in "compared with", "than" after a
comparative ("larger than"), and "of" in "ratio of". Read through the unembedding, its
output points at ratio words ("ratio", "relative", "proportion"), so the negative side
means: a ratio or a comparison is being set up here.

This program predicts a fixed negative value on those connecting words and 0 elsewhere.
The magnitudes are least-squares fits on training text. It is a sketch: nearby words
explain only a sliver of this component's variance.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that, just before "to", make it the "to" of a ratio or a comparison.
RATIO_HEADS = {
    "relative", "relatively", "compared", "proportional", "proportion", "normalized",
    "related", "relation", "ratio", "area", "surface", "volume", "weight", "width",
}
# Comparative adjectives and adverbs that take "than".
COMPARATIVES = {
    "larger", "longer", "higher", "greater", "more", "less", "fewer", "smaller", "bigger",
    "lower", "better", "worse", "faster", "slower", "heavier", "lighter", "closer",
}
# Words whose following "of" or "area" belongs to a ratio.
RATIO_OF = {"ratio", "ratios", "proportion", "percentage"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    if word == "to" and prev in RATIO_HEADS:
        return carry, -0.5
    if word == "per":
        return carry, -0.8
    if word == "-to":
        return carry, -0.9
    if word == "than" and prev in COMPARATIVES:
        return carry, -0.4
    if word == "with" and prev == "compared":
        return carry, -0.9
    if word == "of" and prev in RATIO_OF:
        return carry, -0.9
    if word == "area" and prev == "surface":
        return carry, -1.9
    return carry, 0.0

"""Component 4363 of layers.15.mlp.down_proj: a Wikidata-style relation-predicate detector.

In knowledge-base facts such as "Mont des Cats — located in the administrative territorial entity"
or "neil kensington adam | member of | royal society", the component goes strongly negative on
the words that name the relation: "member of", "located in", "educated at", "instance of",
"shares border with", "time zone", and so on. It fires on the last word of the relation name
(the "of" of "member of", the "in" of "located in", and the "the" that follows "located in").
Its response is stronger when the text just before is full of knowledge-base separators
("|", "—", "->"), and it is near zero on ordinary prose and on most other relations
(birth place, given name, country, occupation, sport), which this program leaves at zero.
"""

READS = ()

# Relation names and their typical activation on their last word (negative = fires).
PREDICATES = {
    "member of": -10,
    "located in": -10,
    "located in the": -10,
    "located on": -9,
    "educated at": -9,
    "participant of": -8,
    "instance of": -6,
    "shares border with": -6,
    "territorial entity": -6,
    "terrain feature": -8,
    "time zone": -5,
    "played on": -5,
    "founded by": -5,
    "located": -4.8,
    "educated": -6.4,
}
KB_SEPARATORS = ("|", "—", "->")
MAX_PHRASE = 5
WINDOW = 100  # tokens looked back for knowledge-base separators


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    words = [s.strip().lower() for s in prefix.token_strings[-MAX_PHRASE:]]
    value = 0.0
    for phrase, v in PREDICATES.items():
        n = len(phrase.split())
        if len(words) >= n and " ".join(words[-n:]) == phrase:
            value = min(value, v)
    if value == 0.0:
        return carry, 0.0
    # How knowledge-base-like the recent text is: separators among the last WINDOW tokens.
    recent = prefix.token_strings[-WINDOW:]
    kb_count = sum(1 for s in recent if s.strip() in KB_SEPARATORS)
    return carry, value * (0.6 + 0.4 * min(1.0, kb_count / 4.0))

"""A rough, readable picture of layer 15's MLP hidden unit 4364 (this component).

The component is that one hidden unit of the MLP that reads layer 15's residual stream
(its value times a fixed norm). Its activation is mostly near zero in prose. In code it is
spiky and mostly negative, and it is larger inside nested brackets. This program keeps only
that coarse picture:

- It counts bracket depth in the current document: ( [ { open a level, ) ] } close one.
- A symbol token (operators and brackets such as = << := + ( { . !) inside brackets
  gets a negative value that grows with depth, capped at depth 3.
- Any other token inside brackets gets a smaller negative value.
- Everywhere else it predicts 0.

The constants are rounded from the mean activation at each depth, measured on training
rows (symbols: about -0.2 to -0.7 at depths 1 to 3+; other tokens: about -0.1). The program
explains very little variance (about 1%): most of the activation is not tied to bracket
depth or to the symbol in front of it.
"""

READS = ()

OPENERS = set("([{")
CLOSERS = set(")]}")
SYMBOLS = set("=<>+-*/%!&|^:.$?(){}[]")

SYMBOL_VALUE = -0.2  # per bracket level, times the depth (capped at 3)
OTHER_VALUE = -0.1  # other tokens inside at least two levels


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    depth, doc = carry if carry is not None else (0, None)
    if prefix.document_ids[-1] != doc:
        depth, doc = 0, prefix.document_ids[-1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    text = token.strip()
    value = 0.0
    if depth >= 1 and text and set(text) <= SYMBOLS:
        value = SYMBOL_VALUE * min(depth, 3)
    elif depth >= 2:
        value = OTHER_VALUE
    for ch in token:
        if ch in OPENERS:
            depth += 1
        elif ch in CLOSERS:
            depth = max(0, depth - 1)
    return (depth, doc), value

"""Layer 15, MLP hidden unit 4365 (this component), read as a word detector.

What the component is: essentially one MLP hidden unit of layer 15. Its input
direction is almost entirely that unit, so its activation is that unit's value
times the norm of its output column. Its output direction, read against the
vocabulary, is noisy; it weakly favours words like "equivalence" and "synonym".

What it responds to: rare, sharp spikes on modular-arithmetic and
equivalence wording: "mod" and especially "modulo" (the largest), "divides",
"congruent", "equivalence", "periodic". Everywhere else it sits near a small
negative background (about -0.03), with no simple lexical pattern. Spikes can
be negative too, in "divide/multiply both sides by" steps, which this program
does not predict.

This program predicts the background value everywhere, and a lexicon weight on
the word itself, where the spike happens. It is a small, honest approximation.
On eval it explains about 0.3% of the variance and leaves the model's output
essentially unchanged (KL fraction 0.99). Token identity cannot explain much
more: a full bigram lookup table reaches only about 1.4% on held-out training
rows.
"""

READS = ()

BACKGROUND = -0.03  # the component's typical value on ordinary tokens

# Typical activation on the word itself, from training text.
LEXICON = {
    "modulo": 10.0,
    "mod": 4.0,
    "equivalence": 3.0,
    "periodic": 2.4,
    "congr": 1.7,
    "divides": 2.0,
    "modular": 1.1,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """The activation at the newest token: a lexicon weight if it is one of the
    modular or equivalence words, otherwise the background value."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    return carry, LEXICON.get(word, BACKGROUND)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Quick check on a sentence: prints the predicted activation per token.
    text = ["x", " mod", " 6", " is", " periodic"]
    for i, tok in enumerate(text):
        word = tok.strip().lower()
        print(f"{tok!r:12} -> {LEXICON.get(word, BACKGROUND)}")

"""Layers.15 MLP down_proj, component 4366: a diffuse, unpredictable readout.

What it does: this component's activation is its read direction dotted with the MLP's
hidden state (6144 units), times its output norm. The read direction's largest single
weight is on hidden unit 4366 of layer 15 (about 10% of the activation's variance), and the
rest is spread over thousands of units. Its activation is close to zero-mean noise
(std 0.28) with no clear concept behind it.

What was checked on 8192 training rows (4.2M positions):
- The current token explains almost none of it (held-out variance explained ~0). Token
  classes (digits, spaces, newlines, CJK, punctuation, latin words) and the previous token's
  class add about 0.2%.
- Position in the document adds almost nothing (the first token of a document is near 0).
- Its activation is autocorrelated within a document (lag-1 about 0.3), but only the
  hidden state can see that, not a token-level rule.
- A linear read of the layer's normalized input explains about 24%, but that is a
  dense 2048-weight map with no human-level meaning.

So the program predicts the component's mean activation everywhere. That is the best
constant (variance explained about 0), and switching the component off already has almost
no effect on the output.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0174  # the component's mean over the eval rows


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 4367 (component 4367 of down_proj), read as a token rule.

The component's activation is almost entirely its neuron's gate-times-up value: silu(gate)
times up-projection of hidden unit 4367 (about 0.9 of it). That value is large and positive
when the unit's gate is open, which happens in the middle of parallel or paired phrasing
("X and Y ... respectively", "both", "between", numbers listed side by side), and is
almost never predictable from the token alone.

This program keeps only the parts a token rule can capture:
- the word "respectively" (and its Chinese counterpart 分别), which reliably gives a large value;
- the percent sign, a moderate value;
- a small value for words and numbers within a short window after a pairing cue
  (and, or, both, between, either, each, versus) in the same document.
Everything else predicts 0. It explains only a small share of the variance.
"""

READS = ()

RESPECTIVE = {"respectively", "respective", "分别"}
PAIR_CUES = {"and", "or", "both", "between", "either", "each", "versus", "vs"} | RESPECTIVE
WINDOW = 8  # tokens after a pairing cue


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = t > 0 and prefix.document_ids[-1] == prefix.document_ids[-2]
    last_cue = carry if (carry is not None and same_doc) else None
    if word in RESPECTIVE:
        value = 3.0
    elif word == "%":
        value = 0.5
    elif last_cue is not None and t - last_cue <= WINDOW and word[:1].isalnum():
        value = 0.1
    else:
        value = 0.0
    if word in PAIR_CUES:
        carry = t
    else:
        carry = last_cue
    return carry, value

"""Position-in-document drift of layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 4368.

This component is a dense linear readout of layer 15's MLP hidden state: its activation
is that hidden state dotted with a fixed direction, the largest weight of which is on
hidden unit 4368 itself (correlation 0.33). That hidden state has no clean token or
concept behind it: token identity explains only about 3% of the variance on held-out
text, and no word class (letters, digits, punctuation, leading space, newline) does
better than about 0.1%. What the activation does show is a slow drift with how far
into its document a token sits. The first token of a document is almost exactly 0, the
next few tokens sit slightly negative, and the activation drifts up to slightly
positive deep into a document. This program predicts that drift from the position
alone, using the mean activation of each position band. On eval it explains about 0.2%
of the variance, which is essentially nothing: it is the simplest honest description of
the component's behaviour, not a full explanation of it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# (first position of a band, mean activation over that band), positions counted
# from the start of the token's own document.
BANDS = (
    (0, 0.0),
    (1, -0.037),
    (2, -0.047),
    (5, -0.029),
    (10, -0.010),
    (30, 0.008),
    (100, 0.020),
    (300, 0.026),
)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):

  document is exactly zero.

  and the longer the repeated run, the higher it goes. Fresh text sits lowest.

READS is empty: this program uses no other component.

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL_ACTIVATION = -0.019
"""The component's mean activation over the eval rows (-0.0191)."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):

What it does: guesses the component's activation from the kind of the current token alone.
Numbers, lowercase word pieces and capitalized words sit slightly above its mean; punctuation
and CJK characters sit slightly below. Each class's value is its mean activation over
about 8,000 training rows (about 4 million tokens).

Why it is this simple: the activation is almost unrelated to surface features. Within one
token the value still varies (std about 0.7 around each token's mean), and neither token
identity, the previous few tokens, a 32-token bag of context, nor word categories explain
more than about 3% of its variance. So this program explains very little, and a per-token
lookup table, which would add about 3%, is not worth its size.

    "number": 0.16,
    "capitalized word": 0.16,
    "word piece": 0.18,
    "space-word": 0.10,
    "other": 0.10,
    "CJK": 0.08,
    "punctuation": 0.06,
}


def token_class(text):
    """The class of one token's text: how it looks, not what it means."""
    if re.fullmatch(r" ?[0-9]+", text):
        return "number"
    if re.fullmatch(r" ?[A-Z][a-z]+", text):
        return "capitalized word"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", text):
        return "word piece"
    if re.fullmatch(r" [a-z]+", text):

    if re.fullmatch(r"\s*[^\w\s]+\s*", text):
        return "punctuation"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, CLASS_MEAN[token_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Activation of the component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4389, a rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP output.

What the component is: its activation is a projection of layer 15's MLP hidden state, and
about 56% of its variance comes from one hidden unit, 4389, whose value is silu(gate) * up.
That unit is large in both directions and spread over ordinary text. No simple rule captures
most of it: a lookup of each token's average value explains only about 3% of the variance
on training text, and a linear bag of the preceding 16 tokens about 1%.

What this program keeps, all of it plain word classes and position:
  - biographical and news/announcement words ("born", "wife", "professor", "announced",
    "recently") and web or contact words ("www", "visit", "website", "links") run high;
  - month and weekday names run moderately high;
  - bare numbers, capitalised names, punctuation and ordinary words run near the baseline,
    with ordinary words slightly below it;
  - the first ~30 tokens of a document run higher than later ones, peaking around token 8.
The predicted value is the class offset plus the position offset, so it is a baseline near
0.1 with those shifts. It explains about 1% of the variance on training text.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MONTHS = set("January February March April May June July August September October November December".split())
WEEKDAYS = set("Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday".split())
WEB = set("www http https website site visit online Twitter blog links link contact email".split())
BIO = set("born died wife husband professor director writer member joined retired executive chairman father mother married".split())
NEWS = set("announced announce recently published currently today yesterday latest launched released excited thank thanks".split())

# Mean offset per word class, from a least-squares fit on training text.
CLASS_OFFSET = {"date": 0.74, "web": 0.90, "bio": 1.29, "news": 1.30,
                "number": -0.15, "name": -0.10, "punct": -0.23, "word": -0.22}

# Offset by tokens since the document started (0, 1, 2-3, 4-7, 8-15, 16-31, 32-63, 64-127, 128-255, 256+).
POSITION_OFFSET = [0.20, 0.26, 0.34, 0.48, 0.52, 0.45, 0.37, 0.32, 0.30, 0.29]
POSITION_EDGES = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]


def word_class(text: str) -> str:
    word = text.strip()
    if word in MONTHS or word in WEEKDAYS:
        return "date"
    if word in WEB or re.search(r"www|http|\.com|://", text):
        return "web"
    if word.lower() in BIO:
        return "bio"
    if word.lower() in NEWS:
        return "news"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\d+", word):
        return "number"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s[A-Z][a-z]+", text):
        return "name"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\W+", word) or not word:
        return "punct"
    return "word"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or doc != carry[0]:
        distance = 0
    else:
        distance = carry[1] + 1
    bin_ = sum(distance >= edge for edge in POSITION_EDGES)
    value = CLASS_OFFSET[word_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])] + POSITION_OFFSET[bin_]
    return (doc, distance), float(value)

"""Dialogue-tag program for layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4391.

The component is mostly the read-out of MLP hidden unit 4391 in layer 15, which is
diffuse and weakly signed across text. Its one clear, strongly negative pattern is a
subject pronoun that starts a dialogue tag right after a closing quotation mark:
    "Ha," I say.      "...," he whispered.
So the program predicts a large negative activation on a subject pronoun (he, she, I,
they, we, it) whose previous token closes a quotation with a comma, full stop, or
!/? (for example ,” or ."), and otherwise predicts the mean activation.
Measured on sample text, this explains only a fraction of a percent of the variance.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.036
TAG_ACTIVATION = -1.5
CLOSING = {',"', ',”', '."', '.”', '!"', '!”', '?"', '?”'}
SUBJECTS = {"he", "she", "i", "they", "we", "it"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    same_doc = prefix.document_ids[-1] == prefix.document_ids[-2]
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    if same_doc and word in SUBJECTS and before in CLOSING:
        return carry, TAG_ACTIVATION
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP, down_proj component 4392: a weak detector of evaluative "method talk".

What the component is: almost exactly MLP hidden unit 4392 of layer 15 (about two thirds of
its variance comes from that one unit). Its activation is near zero on a document's first
token, and mostly small and slightly negative elsewhere, with a heavy negative tail.

What it responds to: the tail is negative on words that praise, compare or recommend a
method, product or option: "better", "best", "efficient", "accurate", "excellent",
"ideal", "advantage", "preferred", "easy", and the nouns they describe, "method",
"approach", "technique", "algorithm". The negative direction of its output promotes
words of that same kind as the next token ("preferred", "advantage", "cheap", "easy").
The effect lingers for a few tokens, so the program also adds a smaller negative value
for each such word among the 12 tokens before.

What the program does: predicts -0.7 on an evaluative word, -0.14 for each one in the
12 tokens before, a baseline of -0.06 elsewhere, and 0 at each document's first token.
This is a fit to the component's mean behaviour, not a full account: on 1024 eval rows
it explains about 0.4% of its variance (Pearson r 0.07). A token-identity table reaches
about 2.6% on held-out training rows, and a causal bag of nearby tokens about 1%, so most
of the variance depends on context that no simple word list captures. Dropping the
baseline makes the variance explained negative, so the baseline is what carries the
small gain. In the model, the program moves the output no more than switching the
component off does (KL fraction about 0.98).
"""

READS = ()

# Words that praise, compare or recommend a method, product or option.
EVALUATIVE = {
    "good", "better", "best", "great", "excellent", "efficient", "effective",
    "accurate", "accuracy", "ideal", "suitable", "useful", "perfect", "optimal",
    "easy", "easier", "nice", "faster", "improved", "recommended", "advantage",
    "advantages", "benefit", "benefits", "preferred", "choice", "option",
}
# Nouns for the methods and approaches being evaluated.
METHODS = {"method", "methods", "approach", "approaches", "technique", "techniques",
           "algorithm", "algorithms", "alternative", "solution"}
WORDS = EVALUATIVE | METHODS

ON_WORD = -0.7      # activation on the evaluative word itself
NEAR_WORD = -0.14   # per evaluative word among the 12 tokens before it
BASELINE = -0.06    # typical value elsewhere


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The first token of a document: the component is silent there.
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    words = [s.strip().lower() for s in prefix.token_strings]
    value = ON_WORD if words[-1] in WORDS else BASELINE
    value += NEAR_WORD * sum(w in WORDS for w in words[-13:-1])
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer-15 MLP unit 4393, the down_proj component 4393, as a sentence-opener detector.

Nearly all of this component's activation is one hidden unit of the layer-15 MLP. That unit
is quiet through most text, but it fires on the first word of a new line (a new paragraph,
a sentence after a heading, a list item) when that word opens a sentence as a determiner,
pronoun, preposition or similar: "The", "In", "We", "It", "This", "With", "When"... It fires
most when the line is a heading or title (no closing punctuation before the break), less
after a sentence that ends in a full stop, less on other capitalised line openers (names,
labels, "Yes"), hardly at all on discourse connectives ("However", "Therefore", "Thus"), and
not at all on sentence starts in the middle of a line. After a line-opening function word its
activity decays over the next few tokens.

The program keeps one number, the tokens since such an opener, and reads each token's value:
  the opener itself, after a heading-like line     -> 4.0
  the opener itself, after a sentence              -> 2.1
  1, 2, 3 tokens after the opener                  -> 1.1, 0.6, 0.3
  other line start, capitalised, not a connective  -> 0.9
  other line start                                 -> 0.2
  everything else                                  -> 0.06
"""

READS = ()

OPENERS = set(
    "The A An In On It We This These Those Our Its His Her Their My Your For If When While "
    "As At After Before There You I He She They With From One Each Here Many Some All Most "
    "Since Because".split()
)
CONNECTIVES = set(
    "However Therefore Thus Alternatively Similarly Also Then Hence Moreover Furthermore "
    "So But And Or Wait Hmm".split()
)
PUNCTUATION = set(".!?:;,")
DECAY = {1: 1.1, 2: 0.6, 3: 0.3}  # activity after an opener, by tokens since it


def _line_end(prefix):
    """The last visible character of the line that ended just before the newest token."""
    text = prefix.token_strings[-2].split("\n")[0].strip()
    j = len(prefix.token_strings) - 3
    while not text and j >= 0:
        text = prefix.token_strings[j].strip()
        j -= 1
    return text[-1:]


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    new_doc = len(prefix.token_strings) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]
    starts_line = not new_doc and "\n" in prefix.token_strings[-2]
    since = None if carry is None or new_doc else carry + 1
    if starts_line:
        since = 0 if word in OPENERS else None
    if since is not None and since > 3:
        since = None
    if since == 0:
        heading = _line_end(prefix) not in PUNCTUATION
        value = 4.0 if heading else 2.1
    elif since is not None:
        value = DECAY[since]
    elif starts_line:
        value = 0.9 if word[:1].isupper() and word not in CONNECTIVES else 0.2
    else:
        value = 0.06
    return since, value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 4394, as seen through down_proj component 4394.

The component's activation is (MLP hidden state . V_c) * ||U_c||. Its input direction
is led by MLP hidden unit 4394 of layer 15 (weight 0.80 of a norm of 1.22), with many
smaller units after it. Its activation is near 0 on most tokens and spikes, positive,
on a few percent of positions (about 1% above 3).

Those spikes lean toward list and structure markers, so this program predicts from the
current token and whether it starts a line:

- ' {"', the brace that opens a JSON object: 5.2 (the strongest single token)
- a bullet or check mark (•, ●, ✓, ✅, ...): 2.0 mid-line, 1.0 at a line start
- a bare digit: 0.1 mid-line, 0.6 at a line start
- a space before an opening bracket: 0.1
- any token that starts a line: +0.4
- everything else: 0

Honest limit: these token classes and line starts explain only about 1-2% of the
variance (eval: variance explained 0.013, r 0.125). The spikes depend on longer
context that a few token rules cannot capture, and the component's end-to-end effect
is tiny (its switched-off KL is 1.2e-5 nats), so this is a coarse map of where it
tends to fire, not a model of what it computes.
"""

READS = ()

BULLETS = set("✓✗✅•●○▪►■□◆↓")
OPENERS = set("{[(")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    stripped = tok.strip()
    new_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    line_start = new_doc or "\n" in prefix.token_strings[-2]
    value = 0.4 if line_start else 0.0
    if tok == ' {"':
        value += 5.0
    elif tok.startswith(" ") and stripped[:1] in OPENERS:
        value += 0.1
    elif stripped and all(c in BULLETS for c in stripped):
        value += 1.0 if line_start else 2.0
    elif stripped.isdigit():
        value += 0.6 if line_start else 0.1
    return carry, value

"""Typical activation of MLP hidden unit 4395 at layer 15, with one small known effect.

The unit's activation is diffuse and context-dependent: no token identity, token
class, position, repetition or model surprisal explains more than about 1% of its
variance. The one consistent pattern is that chat and control markup tokens
(<|im_start|>, <|im_end|>, <|endoftext|>, <think>, <tool_call>, ...) sit slightly
below zero, about -0.18, while every other token averages about +0.02. This program
predicts those two values.

MEAN = 0.02
CONTROL_MEAN = -0.18


def is_control(token: str) -> bool:
    """A markup token such as <|im_start|>, <think> or </tool_call>."""
    return len(token) > 2 and token[0] == "<" and token[-1] == ">" and " " not in token and "\n" not in token


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):

What it is: the component reads MLP hidden unit 4396 of layer 15 (its V vector is
about 45% that unit, the rest a diffuse mix of other units). Its activation is
roughly a zero-centred value with std 0.36 that depends on context, not on the

10M tokens) and switching it off barely changes the model's output.

What this program does: it predicts the component's average activation at every
position, a constant near its mean (-0.02). Nothing simple in the text (token
identity, token class, previous token, position in the document) explains the
variation: those features give test R^2 <= 0, so a constant is the honest
readable answer.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.02


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):

    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 4397, read through its down_proj component.

The component's input weight is mostly on that one MLP hidden unit (about 70% of its
energy), and its output direction promotes words like "supporters", "followers",
"devoted" and "supportive". Plain-terms summary: the unit rests slightly below zero
almost everywhere. It rises in text about organisations and communities (community,
association, society, church, foundation, institute, followers, volunteers, ...), and
it stays a little raised for a few tokens after such a word. This program predicts
exactly that: a resting value, a jump on organisation/community words, and a decaying
memory of them within the same document. It explains only a small share of the
variance: most of the unit's activity is not captured by words or word context.
"""

READS = ()

RESTING = -0.05
"""Typical value away from any organisation words (the unit's mean is about -0.05)."""

ORG_WORDS = frozenset(
    """community communities association associations society societies church churches
    institute institutions foundation foundations union unions party parties club clubs
    family families followers follower fans volunteers volunteer donations donation
    organization organizations organisation network forum website websites links link
    international national congregation fundraising fundraiser charity charities league
    federation council committee alliance coalition movement members member initiative
    campaign program programs project support supporters supporter devoted devote raise
    group groups company companies corporation""".split()
)
"""Words for organisations, communities and groups of supporters."""

ORG_JUMP = 0.6
"""Predicted rise on an organisation word itself."""

MEMORY_DECAY = 0.95
"""How much of the organisation context survives each token."""

MEMORY_WEIGHT = 0.1
"""Predicted rise per unit of decayed organisation context."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    new_document = len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    memory = 0.0 if carry is None or new_document else carry
    is_org = word in ORG_WORDS
    value = RESTING + ORG_JUMP * is_org + MEMORY_WEIGHT * memory

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 4398: a chat-markup detector, with a weak
knowledge-graph-list term.

Plain-terms summary: this component is near zero on most text. It fires on the markup
of Qwen's chat and tool-calling format: strongest on the start of a chat turn
(`<|im_start|>`) and on the opening of a reasoning block (`<think>`), weaker on the
tool-call and tool-response tags, and near zero on the end-of-turn tag `<|im_end|>`
(slightly positive when it closes a tool call). The first token of a document has no
context before it, so it reads as zero.

Inside dense lists of knowledge-graph triples ("entity | relation | entity", or "->"
and "—" separators), ordinary tokens drift mildly positive: a small extra term.

The program predicts, for each position, a fixed activation per marker token (the mean
the component shows on that marker in training text), about 0.5 on ordinary tokens
when at least two triple separators sit in the previous 64 tokens of the document, and
0 elsewhere. It captures most of the output effect of switching the component off
(about 88% of the KL), but only about a fifth of the variance, because the component's
many small activations on ordinary text are not explained by any simple rule.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Typical activation on each marker token, mid-document.
MARKER_ACTIVATION = {
    "<think>": 10.9,  # opens the reasoning block, after "assistant\n"
    "<|im_start|>": 9.7,  # starts a chat turn, after a newline
    "<tool_response>": 7.2,  # opens a tool's output
    "</tool_call>": 4.0,  # closes a tool call
    "</tool_response>": 3.7,  # closes a tool's output
}
TOOL_CALL_AFTER_NEWLINE = 6.4  # "<tool_call>" right after a newline
TOOL_CALL_OTHER = 3.4  # "<tool_call>" after other text, such as ":"
IM_END_AFTER_TOOL_CALL = 1.0  # "<|im_end|>" closing a tool call: slightly positive
IM_END_OTHER = -0.8  # "<|im_end|>" closing ordinary text: slightly negative

# Separators between the parts of a knowledge-graph triple, as in "a | b | c".
SEPARATORS = {" |", " ->", " —"}
WINDOW = 64  # tokens looked back over
KG_VALUE = 0.5  # typical activation of an ordinary token inside such a list


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    token = prefix.token_strings[t]
    previous = prefix.token_strings[t - 1] if t > 0 else ""
    new_doc = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]
    # Positions of the triple separators within the last WINDOW tokens of this document.
    recent = [] if new_doc else [i for i in carry if i > t - WINDOW]
    if token in SEPARATORS:
        recent.append(t)
    if new_doc:  # no context before the first token of a document
        return recent, 0.0
    if token == "<tool_call>":
        value = TOOL_CALL_AFTER_NEWLINE if previous == "\n" else TOOL_CALL_OTHER
    elif token == "<|im_end|>":
        value = IM_END_AFTER_TOOL_CALL if previous == "</tool_call>" else IM_END_OTHER
    elif token in MARKER_ACTIVATION:
        value = MARKER_ACTIVATION[token]
    elif token not in SEPARATORS and len(recent) >= 2:
        value = KG_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return recent, float(value)

text is naming a second party to a comparison, competition or pairing: "other"/"another"
used as a counterpart ("interact with other companies", "compareTo(other)"), words such as
compare, competitor, rival, peer, fellow, opponent, equal, different, and the pairing words
between / against / versus. It is near zero elsewhere. The sign is the important part:
the component's output, scaled by a negative activation, pushes the next-token
distribution toward comparison and peer words ("comparison", "compare", "other", "sharing").

# "other"/"another" as a counterpart noun.
COUNTERPART = re.compile(r"^(other|others|another)$", re.I)
# Pairing words.
PAIRING = re.compile(r"^(between|against|versus|vs)$", re.I)
TWO = re.compile(r"^(two|both)$", re.I)
WITH = re.compile(r"^with$", re.I)
# Words after which a counterpart is a second party to an interaction.

    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()

        value = -1.65 if before in PREPOSITIONS else -0.85
    elif COMPARISON.search(word):
        value = -1.1
    elif PAIRING.match(word):
        value = -0.55
    elif TWO.match(word):
        value = -0.22
    elif WITH.match(word):
        value = -0.17
    else:

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:4400.

This is one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its input direction is
mostly MLP hidden unit 4400 of layer 15 (that unit's contribution carries about 71% of
the component's variance), and its output direction, read through the unembedding,
promotes citation-field tokens such as "pp", "vol", "doi", "isbn" and "pages" when its
activation is negative. So it is a "reference-list / number-expected" feature: it goes
negative in bibliographic entries and number-dense text, and mildly positive in licence
and boilerplate text.

The program reads only the recent tokens of the current document and writes a small
linear score built from concepts:
  - bibliographic words nearby (journal, publisher, pp, vol, doi, press, ...)  -> negative
  - licence / legal boilerplate words nearby                                    -> positive
  - digits in the last few tokens, and whether this token starts or continues a number -> mixed
  - the current token being punctuation or a space, especially inside a citation -> negative

It captures only a little of the activation: the big negative spikes are sparse and
depend on context this short window does not see. Coefficients are least-squares fits to
the component's activations on training rows.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

WINDOW = 12
"""How many recent tokens of the current document the score looks back over."""

BIBLIOGRAPHY = re.compile(
    r"(pp|vol|no|doi|isbn|pages?|pg|eds?|journal|proc|proceedings|press|springer|ieee"
    r"|trans\w*|publish\w*|univ\w*|phys|sci|soc|chem|bull|lett\w*|acad\w*|review|math\w*"
    r"|biol\w*|med|appl\w*|ibid|arxiv)"
)
"""Words that show a bibliographic reference: journal, publisher and page/volume fields."""

LICENCE = re.compile(r"(licen[sc]\w*|apache|unless|basis|copyright|warrant\w*)")
"""Licence and legal boilerplate words."""


def _word(token: str) -> str:
    return token.strip().lower().strip(".,()[]")


def _is_digit(token: str) -> bool:
    return token.strip().isdigit()


def _is_space(token: str) -> bool:
    return token.strip() == "" and token != ""


def _is_punct(token: str) -> bool:
    s = token.strip()
    return s != "" and all(not c.isalnum() and c != "_" for c in s)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    doc = ids[-1]
    recent = []
    for i in range(len(ids) - 1, -1, -1):
        if ids[i] != doc or len(recent) == WINDOW:
            break
        recent.append(prefix.token_strings[i])
    # recent[0] is the current token, recent[1] the one before it, and so on.
    cur = recent[0]
    prev = recent[1] if len(recent) > 1 else ""
    last3 = recent[:3]
    last6 = recent[:6]

    bib12 = sum(bool(BIBLIOGRAPHY.fullmatch(_word(t))) for t in recent)
    bib3 = sum(bool(BIBLIOGRAPHY.fullmatch(_word(t))) for t in last3)
    lic12 = sum(bool(LICENCE.fullmatch(_word(t))) for t in recent)
    dig6 = sum(_is_digit(t) for t in last6)
    bib_near = 1.0 if bib12 else 0.0

    digit_now = 1.0 if _is_digit(cur) else 0.0
    starts_number = 1.0 if digit_now and not _is_digit(prev) else 0.0
    continues_number = 1.0 if digit_now and _is_digit(prev) else 0.0
    punct_now = 1.0 if _is_punct(cur) else 0.0
    space_now = 1.0 if _is_space(cur) else 0.0

    value = (
        0.028
        - 0.045 * bib12
        - 0.168 * bib3
        - 0.083 * dig6
        + 0.106 * starts_number
        + 0.041 * continues_number
        - 0.136 * punct_now
        + 0.099 * lic12
        - 0.335 * punct_now * bib_near
        - 0.515 * space_now * bib_near
        - 0.033 * digit_now * bib_near
        - 0.315 * dig6 * bib_near
    )
    return carry, float(value)

Plain-language reading. Most of the time this component is small (typically
within +-0.5), with no clear token pattern: a token's identity explains only about
2% of its variance, and nearby tokens explain little more. Its largest negative
values (below -3) fall on a head noun right after "a" or "an" that the model
expects to be followed by a complement, as in "a way [to]", "a method [of]",
"a manner [in which]", "a device [that]", "a rate [that]". Its largest positive
values fall on words that come right before a noun slot.

This program captures only the first pattern, as a rough guide:
  - a generic head noun right after "a"/"an" -> -1.0
  - any other noun right after "a"/"an"      -> -0.1
  - everything else                          -> 0
It reads only the prefix, one token at a time. It explains almost none of the
variance (about 0.1%): the component's activation is not captured by such rules.

import wordnet

READS = ()

ARTICLES = {"a", "an"}
GENERIC_NOUNS = {
    "way", "manner", "method", "device", "material", "program", "rate", "system",
    "place", "point", "set", "value", "process", "number", "amount", "kind", "type",
    "form", "means", "procedure", "technique", "approach", "mechanism", "function",
    "algorithm", "formula", "structure", "tool", "machine", "model", "design",
    "strategy", "solution", "object", "thing", "substance", "class", "item", "unit",
    "measure", "framework", "product", "situation", "position", "area", "line",
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if len(prefix.token_strings) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return carry, 0.0
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower()
    if before not in ARTICLES or not word.isalpha():
        return carry, 0.0
    if word in GENERIC_NOUNS:
        return carry, -1.0
    if "noun" in wordnet.parts_of_speech(word):

    return carry, 0.0

It fires on the word "or" when it joins alternatives ("read or write", "fees or
expenses"), and on the same word in other languages ("oder", "ou", "или", "或",

"""German function words in German running text, for one MLP output direction (layer 15,
component 4403).

What the component does, in plain terms: it is silent in most text. It fires on German
function words that sit inside a clause, such as prepositions (in, bei, für, nach, seit,
mit, von) and focus or modal particles (schon, nur, auch, noch, immer, erst, so). It fires
hardest when the word comes straight after an auxiliary verb or a pronoun, as in
"... ist [in] ...", "... wird [seit] ...", "... hat [auf] den ...", "... sich [bei] ...".
Its activation is near zero in English, code, and other scripts.

The program, for each token:
  1. Is the token a German preposition or particle from the lists below? If not, predict 0.
  2. How German is the recent text? Over the last 32 words of the same document, the share
     of words that wordfreq counts as German rather than English (the "German share"). Only
     the part above 0.3 counts.
  3. Does the token follow an auxiliary verb or a pronoun? If so, the prediction is 4 times
     larger.
The prediction is 2.5 * (German share - 0.3) * (1 or 4).

It is a coarse description. On 1,024 training rows it explains about 2% of the activation's
variance, with a correlation of about 0.15. Most of the variance is in many small values
spread over ordinary text, which no short rule describes. The spikes it does capture are
the component's largest ones.
"""

from functools import lru_cache

import regex
import wordfreq

READS = ()

PREPOSITIONS = frozenset(
    "in im an am auf aus bei beim bis durch für gegen nach seit trotz um unter über von vom "
    "vor wegen zu zum zur mit ohne während zwischen".split()
)
PARTICLES = frozenset(
    "schon immer erst nur gleich nun hier ganz auch als wohl selbst viel doch sehr so noch "
    "ab wie wieder gar mehr etwas eben ja halt".split()
)
AUXILIARIES_AND_PRONOUNS = frozenset(
    "ist sind war waren wird werden wurde wurden hat haben hatte is are was were will would "
    "can may has have had sich sie er es ich wir ihn ihm ihr mich mir du".split()
)
WINDOW = 32
THRESHOLD = 0.3
WEIGHT = 2.5


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def language(token):
    """+1 if the token is a word wordfreq counts as German, -1 if English, else 0."""
    word = token.strip().lower()
    if not regex.fullmatch(r"\p{L}{2,}", word):
        return 0
    de = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(word, "de")
    en = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(word, "en")
    if de > en + 0.5 and de > 3:
        return 1
    if en > de + 0.5 and en > 3:
        return -1
    return 0


def german_share(prefix):
    """Share of German among the recent words of the same document that are German or English."""
    t = prefix.position
    german = english = 0
    for j in range(max(0, t - WINDOW + 1), t + 1):
        if prefix.document_ids[j] != prefix.document_ids[t]:
            continue
        kind = language(prefix.token_strings[j])
        german += kind == 1
        english += kind == -1
    return german / (german + english) if german + english else 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[t].strip().lower()
    if word not in PREPOSITIONS and word not in PARTICLES:
        return carry, 0.0
    if t == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    share = german_share(prefix)
    if share <= THRESHOLD:
        return carry, 0.0
    previous = prefix.token_strings[t - 1].strip().lower()
    same_document = prefix.document_ids[t - 1] == prefix.document_ids[t]
    after_verb_or_pronoun = same_document and previous in AUXILIARIES_AND_PRONOUNS
    value = WEIGHT * (share - THRESHOLD) * (4.0 if after_verb_or_pronoun else 1.0)
    return carry, float(value)

(about 77% of its norm), and its output direction, read through the embeddings (a
logit-lens guess), promotes definitional continuations such as " (", "是指" ("refers to")
and "以下简称" ("hereinafter called") when its activation is negative. Its large negative

expansion or gloss is likely to follow, e.g. "EEDI" and "RPE" before " (".

What this program predicts:
- a negative value right after a gloss cue ("refers to", "i.e.", "e.g.", "also called",
  "known as", "meaning", "stands for", "short for", "abbreviated"), where a definition
  comes next;
- a negative value on acronym-like tokens (all capitals, two or more letters), larger when
  the acronym is first mentioned in its document, and a smaller one on the token right
  after an acronym.

component's strong negatives, and its activation is mostly unpredictable from its prefix.

GLOSS_CUES = (
    "refers to", "i.e", "e.g", "also called", "known as", "meaning", "stands for",
    "short for", "abbreviated",
)
GLOSS_VALUE = -0.18
FIRST_ACRONYM = -0.12
REPEAT_ACRONYM = -0.08
AFTER_ACRONYM = -0.07


def is_acronym(text):
    """All capitals, letters only, at least two of them, e.g. 'GVWR', 'EEDI', 'AI'."""
    text = text.strip()
    return len(text) >= 2 and text.isalpha() and text.isupper()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (acronyms seen so far in the current document, whether the last token was one)
    seen, prev_acronym = carry if carry is not None else (set(), False)
    new_doc = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if new_doc:
        seen, prev_acronym = set(), False
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    recent = "".join(prefix.token_strings[-3:]).lower()

        value = GLOSS_VALUE

    return (seen, is_acronym(token)), value

In plain terms: this component's activation is small (std about 0.28) and its
sign is roughly even. It barely depends on which token is present or where it
sits in the text, and it almost never matters to the model's output (switching
it off changes next-token predictions by about 1e-6 nats). The few regularities
found are used here:

1. The first token of each document is silent (activation about 0).
2. Tokens 2 to 8 of a document lean slightly positive, and tokens 9 to 32 a bit less.
3. Whole words lean up or down depending on how common they are: rarer words
   read slightly positive, common words slightly negative.
4. Newlines lean slightly negative; tokens containing digits lean slightly positive.

These are a linear fit of the features above on 16k training rows. It explains
under 1% of the variance on held-out rows, so it is a description of the weak
trend, not a predictor. A per-token lookup table reaches about 3 to 4%, but it
is a table of arbitrary token ids, so it is left out.

import regex
import wordfreq

WEIGHTS = {
    "baseline": -0.023,
    "first_token": 0.003,
    "tokens_2_to_8": 0.076,
    "tokens_9_to_32": 0.017,
    "is_word": 0.065,
    "word_zipf": -0.009,
    "newline": -0.032,
    "has_digit": 0.035,
}

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or doc != carry[0]:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1

    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = tok.strip()
    is_word = regex.fullmatch(r"\p{L}+", word) is not None
    zipf = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(word.lower(), "en") if is_word else 0.0

    value = WEIGHTS["baseline"]
    if pos == 0:
        value += WEIGHTS["first_token"]
    if 2 <= pos <= 8:
        value += WEIGHTS["tokens_2_to_8"]
    elif 9 <= pos <= 32:
        value += WEIGHTS["tokens_9_to_32"]
    if is_word:
        value += WEIGHTS["is_word"] + WEIGHTS["word_zipf"] * zipf
    if "\n" in tok:
        value += WEIGHTS["newline"]

    return (doc, pos), float(value)

EARLY = {0: 0.0, 1: -0.78, 2: -0.29, 3: -0.19, 4: -0.11}
DEFAULT = 0.01
REPEAT_BONUS = 0.07

    docs = prefix.document_ids

    if carry is None or len(docs) < 2 or docs[-1] != docs[-2]:

Its activation is almost entirely one MLP hidden unit: unit 4412 of layer 15
(its input direction is ~0.9 on that unit). It sits near zero on most tokens.
It goes clearly negative on prepositions and conjunctions that open an adverbial

"until", "after", "with", "but", "when", and their equivalents in other
languages (ohne, sans, avec, без, bez, 但是, 直到, ...). The most negative are
"before", "without" and "until".

training text, when the token is one of these connectives; every other token
gets 0. A connective that starts a sentence is predicted a bit more strongly.

(r = 0.18). The rest depends on context a word list cannot see.
"""

READS = ()

# Mean activation of each connective (training text), grouped by strength.
STRONG = {  # clause-opening "before / without / until / after" type words
    "before": -3.0, "without": -2.8, "until": -2.8, "till": -2.6, "after": -1.7,
    "prior": -1.1, "ohne": -3.9, "без": -3.4, "bez": -2.1, "sans": -1.9,
    "avec": -1.9, "dank": -3.9, "由于": -2.2, "直到": -2.6, "截至": -5.2,
    "但是": -2.4, "没有": -1.9, "после": -1.8, "absent": -2.6,
}
MILD = {  # "with / but / when / since" type words
    "with": -0.7, "but": -0.7, "when": -0.9, "since": -0.6, "if": -0.3,
    "however": -0.5, "mit": -1.3, "pre": -1.1, "con": -0.7, "с": -0.7,
    "但": -1.6, "在": -0.6, "与": -1.1, "如果": -1.3, "之前": -1.3,
}
SENTENCE_END = set(".!?;:\n。！？；")
BOOST = 1.6  # a connective opening a sentence is predicted this much more strongly


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the newest token's activation from its connective class and position."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    value = STRONG.get(word, MILD.get(word, 0.0))
    if value and len(prefix.token_strings) > 1:
        if prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() in SENTENCE_END:
            value *= BOOST
    elif value:
        value *= BOOST  # first token of a row
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 4414: a diffuse, near-zero feature with no readable trigger.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the MLP's down projection. It reads the MLP hidden
state through a direction that is mostly hidden unit 4414 (about a third of its squared norm)
plus a spread of many other hidden units, and writes a tiny amount into the residual stream.

What the data shows (4M training tokens):
  - Its activation is signed, centred near 0, with std about 0.30, and is almost never sparse.
  - It does not depend on the current token: a per-token lookup explains about 2% of the
    variance on held-out text, and token classes (punctuation, digits, CJK, prepositions,
    negation words, code-like tokens) explain under 0.5%.
  - It does not depend on position in the document, apart from the first token of each
    document, where it is always about 0.
  - It does not track the model's own uncertainty (entropy, surprisal and top-1 probability
    all have |r| < 0.02). Its only strong correlate is hidden unit 4414 itself (r = 0.41).
  - Causal importance is essentially zero everywhere (mean 1.3e-7), so switching it off barely
    changes the model's next-token predictions.

So the program predicts the component's mean value at every token, and 0 at the first token
of each document. This explains about 0% of the variance. It is the honest simple version:
no short readable rule captures this component's activation.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.01
"""The component's average activation over tokens."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """The activation at this position: 0 at a document's first token, else the mean."""
    first_of_document = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or (
        prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    )
    return carry, 0.0 if first_of_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15, MLP down_proj, component 4415.

What it does: a mostly-negative detector for punctuation that sets up a value or an
expression to come next. It is most negative on colons that introduce a value (``key: value``
in code, logs and prints; ``":`` and ``':`` in JSON-like text), strongly negative on
assignment and arrow signs (`` =``, ``=``, `` =>``, `` :=``, a colon ending a line),
and mildly negative on opening brackets, braces and parentheses and on dashes and pipes.
It is positive on the opening of a JSON-style object (`` {"``). Every other token sits
near zero, with small noise.

Why: the component's activation is set mainly by the token just read, and these punctuation
classes carry most of its large values. Keying on them is the simplest description of what
it responds to. The numbers are each class's mean activation over a sample of training text.
What it leaves out: the diffuse part of the activation on ordinary words, which is
context-dependent and which no simple token rule (or a linear bag of context tokens) captures.

Main program: `step` looks up the newest token's string in the four classes and returns that
class's value, or 0 for any other token. It keeps no state.
"""

READS = ()

# Colons that introduce a value, including JSON-style and code-style forms.
COLON = {":", '":', "':", " :", "：", '\\":', ":\\", "):", "`:", "**:"}
# Equals and arrow signs, and a colon ending a line.
ASSIGN = {" =", "=", " :=", " =>", "=>", "={", ":\n", ":\n\n"}
# Opening brackets, dashes and pipes.
OPEN = {" (", " [", " {", " ->", " —", " |", " ${"}
# The opening of a JSON-style object is positive.
JSON_OPEN = {' {"'}

CLASS_VALUE = {}
for _tok in COLON:
    CLASS_VALUE[_tok] = -1.6
for _tok in ASSIGN:
    CLASS_VALUE[_tok] = -0.9
for _tok in OPEN:
    CLASS_VALUE[_tok] = -0.5
for _tok in JSON_OPEN:
    CLASS_VALUE[_tok] = 1.7


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Activation at the newest token: its class value, or 0 for any other token."""
    return carry, float(CLASS_VALUE.get(prefix.token_strings[-1], 0.0))
